title: Edge connection demultiplex & fanout collapse retrospective (P0) - Hosted API streaming outage
content:
Summary:
On 2028-06-13 03:42 UTC we observed a P0 outage affecting Hosted API streaming sessions. Symptoms included: widespread streaming stalls (clients saw no tokens for 10-60s), elevated 5xx rates from edge proxies, and a sharp drop in successful streaming throughput. Impact: ~15% of streaming sessions experienced persistent stalls; overall hosted-api tail latency (p99) for streaming requests rose from ~210ms to >2.5s during the peak. Several customer integrations retried and generated downstream load spikes.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 03:37 - Small uptick in edge per-connection queue depth alert (auto-alert threshold marginally triggered).
- 03:42 - Rapid escalation: error-rate alert from edge proxies firing (5xx rate > 2%). First on-call page.
- 03:45 - Initial triage: many streaming sessions in ESTABLISHED state but not emitting tokens; HTTP/2 streams stuck waiting for backend responses.
- 03:50 - SRE attempted soft mitigation: increase edge proxy worker pool on two regions; temporary reduction in 5xx but stalls persisted.
- 04:05 - Engineering change identified: rollout of demultiplexer refactor (edge-proxy v3.8.1) started at 02:55 with canary, graduated to region-wide at 03:30.
- 04:12 - Rollback of v3.8.1 initiated for region A; immediate reduction in 5xx but streaming stall rate remained non-trivial due to queued sessions.
- 04:30 - Additional mitigation: enable short-circuit session drop for idle streams > 45s and restart edge workers to flush stuck queues.
- 05:10 - Incident declared resolved for most customers; post-incident stabilization continued through 12:00.

Root cause (summary):
A logic bug introduced by the demultiplexer refactor in edge-proxy v3.8.1 changed how long-lived streaming connections were assigned to worker shards. Under typical multiplexed load the new logic created imbalanced session affinity: a minority of worker threads received a disproportionate number of long-lived streams (head-of-line sessions). Those overloaded workers experienced thread starvation and queue buildup. When those workers fell behind, they produced timeouts and 5xx responses back to the central routing layer, which then retried or fanout more aggressively to other nodes (legacy retry/fanout heuristics), amplifying CPU and queue pressure across the edge cluster and causing a collapse in effective fanout and throughput.

Contributing factors:
- The demux refactor passed unit tests and component-level integration tests but lacked a realistic, long-lived streaming multi-tenant canary harness that exercises sustained affinity skew.
- Canary rollout window was short for the change; graduation criteria relied on error-rate (which was initially low) instead of per-worker queue depth or skew metrics.
- Autoscaler and circuit-breaker thresholds were not tuned for sudden hotspot imbalance: retries and fallback fanout rules amplified the failure instead of damping it.
- Observability gap: we lacked a direct alert for per-worker session skew (sessions-per-worker p99) and per-worker CPU queue backlog.

Why the behavior looked like 5xx/latency rather than an obvious bug in demux: overloaded workers produced resource exhaustion and transient internal errors and timeouts; the central router interpreted those as endpoint failures and retried/fanned out, creating larger pressure.

Immediate mitigations taken during incident:
- Rollback of edge-proxy v3.8.1 in affected regions (03:50 - 04:12) — reduced new error surface.
- Scale-up: added additional edge worker pools and restarted edge processes to flush backlog (03:52 - 04:20).
- Apply temporary throttle on retries and limit fanout concurrency from the central router (04:00) to break amplification loop.
- Implemented emergency short-circuit: drop idle streaming sessions >45s and return structured error to clients to avoid stuck sockets (04:30).
- Communications: status-page updates, customer-facing banner for high-latency streaming (04:05 - 04:45).

Detection and monitoring notes:
- The earliest signal that should have been actionable was the per-edge queue depth trend (sustained upward slope starting ~03:37). That metric was present in Grafana but not surfaced to the auto-alert policy.
- Existing SLO alerts were based on p99 latency and global 5xx rate; both lagged the worker-level skew metric in this failure mode.

Impact quantification (rough):
- Peak affected streaming sessions: ~15% of total streaming active sessions across regions (approx. 18k concurrent sessions).
- Peak global 5xx rate for streaming endpoints: 3.6% for a 14-minute window.
- Additional compute cost due to retries/fanout during incident: estimated +22% over baseline for edge fleet during 03:45-04:15.

Runbook updates (draft):
We need a concrete runbook entry for "edge demultiplexer imbalance". Draft steps below (short form, to be codified into the runbook playbook).
- Detection: Grafana panel 'edge.worker.session-skew' breach (p99 sessions-per-worker > 2x median) OR per-worker queue depth > 75% of queue capacity for >2m.
- Immediate triage: identify worker IDs with highest queue depth (edge admin command: /admin/edge/workers?region=R - include sessions, cpu, queue_depth).
- Mitigation path A (if change recently rolled): rollback last edge-proxy deployment -> verify per-worker skew reduces in 3-7 minutes.
- Mitigation path B (if overloaded due to traffic): scale edge worker group + restart workers gracefully (drain + restart) to rebalance assignment.
- Break amplification: temporarily set central-router.retry-fanout-max=1 and disable speculative retries for streaming endpoints.
- If stuck sessions remain: trigger short-circuit drop with structured error and record session ids for follow-up analysis.
- Communications: post initial incident on #sre-incidents, notify product and CS leads, update status page.

Longer-term actions and owners (priority & target dates):
- Add per-worker skew and queue-depth alert to on-call SLOs (owner: Marcus Liu, target: 2028-07-01).
- Rework demultiplexer: add fairness heuristic and backpressure propagation to central router to prevent fanout amplification (owner: Sofia Reyes, target: 2028-06-30).
- Add a long-lived streaming canary harness that simulates biased affinity and sustained sessions (owner: Aisha Patel, target: 2028-06-22).
- Improve rollout policy: require 2-hour canary with skew and queue metrics gating before full graduation (owner: Eng Release, Liam O'Connor, target: 2028-06-25).
- Tune autoscaler and circuit-breaker thresholds to limit retry amplification under partial worker degradation (owner: Zara Ahmed, target: 2028-06-28).
- Post-incident retrospective doc & blameless write-up to customers with timeline and compensation options (owner: Evan Brooks, target: 2028-06-20).

Testing and validation plan for fixes:
- Unit + integration tests for demux fairness under synthetic skewed load.
- Synthetic chaos test: recover a random subset of edge workers to confirm system stability without retry amplification.
- Canary experiments with traffic shadowing for 24h to confirm no hidden skew.

Lessons learned (blameless):
- Complex refactors touching long-lived session assignment require realistic long-running canaries; unit tests alone are insufficient.
- Amplification rules (retries/fanout) are a common multiplier—fail-open retry policies will need stricter damping for streaming paths.
- Observability should be targeted at the unit-of-failure (worker) not only at aggregated edges; short-lived p99s can mask worker-level collapse.

Follow-ups and owners (one-line):
- Marcus Liu -> add and tune per-worker alerts (2028-07-01).
- Sofia Reyes -> demux fairness patch + PR review (2028-06-30).
- Aisha Patel -> implement streaming canary harness + docs (2028-06-22).
- Liam O'Connor -> rollout gating and release checklist change (2028-06-25).
- Zara Ahmed -> circuit-breaker tuning and simulated failure tests (2028-06-28).
- Evan Brooks -> customer-facing incident summary and compensation recommendation (2028-06-20).

Open questions (for next incident review):
- Should the central-router implement adaptive backoff on detection of worker skew rather than static retry caps?
- What is the optimal canary duration for long-lived streaming changes? 2h vs 24h?
- How to best surface per-worker skew in the on-call pager without creating too many noisy alerts?

Appendix: useful commands and quick references (to be moved into runbook):
- List edge workers and queue depths: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://edge-admin.redwood/v1/workers?region=<R>
- Set central router retry cap (temporary): kubectl -n router set env deployment/router CENTRAL_RETRY_FANOUT_MAX=1
- Rollback edge-proxy deployment: kubectl -n edge rollout undo deployment/edge-proxy --to-revision=<previous-rev>
- Restart edge worker gracefully: kubectl -n edge rollout restart deployment/edge-worker-<shard>

Blameless note:
No individual is blamed. The root cause chain is a combination of a logic regression, insufficient canary coverage for long-lived sessions, and amplification via retry/fanout heuristics. We focus on systems fixes and process changes to prevent recurrence.

Next steps: finalize this draft, request engineering sign-off on the demux fix PR, add the runbook entry, and schedule the canary harness work.
